line: I feel like Toussaint, I feel like Boukman
vault_lines: I feel like Toussaint, I feel like Boukman
meaning: Two important figures in the history of the Haitian Revolution were Toussiant L'Ouverture and Dutty Boukman. L'Ouverture was a major general in the Haitian Revolution, the largest slave rebellion since that of Spartacus 1900 years earlier and only the nation in the history of the world to be established through a succesful slave rebellion. On the night of August 14, 1791, representative slaves from nearby plantations gathered to participate in a secret ceremony (Bois Caiman) conducted in the woods by nearby Le Cap in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. Presided over by Dutty Boukman, a prominent slave leader and Vodou priest (houngan}, the ceremony served as both a religious ritual and strategic meeting as conspirators met and planned a revolt against the ruling white planters of the colony’s wealthy Northern Plain. The ceremony is considered the official beginning of the Haitian Revolution. Kodak recalls these events and compares himself to both figures in relation to his Haitian heritage.

line: Jamestown, Virginia, slavery started and it’s still there 2019, we’ll be free after 400 years
vault_lines: Jamestown, Virginia, slavery started and it's still there
meaning:
In August 1619, 20 enslaved Angolans arrived in Jamestown, in the British colony of Virginia and were traded to the privateer The White Lion for food. This transaction marks the first time that enslaved Africans were sold in North America, setting the stage for more than two centuries of slavery.

Kodak has previously approached the idea that slavery still exists nowadays—despite its official abolition with the 13th Amendment in 1865—in a June 2017 tweet.

Kodak, who is known for being a spiritual person, refers to the Bible and alludes to Acts 7:6, in which God said to Abram:

Your descendants will be strangers in a foreign land, where they will be in slavery and oppressed for four hundred years.

Following Kodak’s reasoning, 1619 being the date when slavery started, 2019 would mark the end of the 400-years bondage described by God in Acts 7:6. Kodak has previously alluded to this theory in Dreezy’s October 2017 song “Spar”:

But they only got two more years of slavery to do harm to us

This is a callback to Kodak Black’s March 2017 song “Conscience.” The song features Atlanta rapper Future and finds Kodak rapping:

These streets made me lose my conscience, took a nigga soul

line: So I went out to the club Can’t drink ’cause I’m too young, but today I’m getting drunk
vault_lines: Can't drink 'cause I'm too young, but today I'm getting drunk
meaning:
Kodak Black is 22 years old at the time of the release of “Harriet Tubman.” The Florida drinking age is the same as the national drinking age, which is 21.

Kodak Black has criticized alcohol legislation before on Dreezy’s October 2017 song “Spar”:

Ain’t old enough to hit the club and fill my cup with rum
But I can go die in the army, goin' to war for them
Ain’t old enough for marijuana cigars, or spark my blunt
But old enough to spend my life behind bars, that’s dumb

Kodak reflects on his tough come-up and draws a parallel between his life and that of Harriet Tubman (1822 – 1913), who was an American civil rights activist. Born into slavery, Tubman became one of the first runaway slaves to lead a wave of abolitionism by escaping slavery in 1849 before conducting missions to rescue approximatively 70 enslaved people through the 19th century.



Kodak similarly considers himself an activist and had to go through years of hustle and run-ins with federal authorities before finding success in his life.

Kodak has previously used this comparison on his August 2017 song “Change My Ways”:

Harriet Tubman, I’m still on the run
